title: The Fir Tree

full_text:
Out in the deep green forest grew a charming little fir tree. It occupied a delightful spot, where the sun warmed its branches, the breeze played through its needles, and many taller pine and spruce companions grew around it.

Yet the little fir tree was thoroughly discontented. It thought of nothing but growing taller: "Oh, if only I were a tall, majestic tree like my elders! The birds would build nests in my boughs, and when the wind blew, I could nod with aristocratic grandeur!"

The sweet sunshine, the gentle breeze, and the merry country children who gathered wild strawberries around its trunk meant nothing to the impatient tree. "Grow! Grow! That is the only thing worth living for!" it sighed.

In autumn, woodcutters arrived and felled several of the tallest pines. The swallows and storks told the fir tree that the great trunks were made into masts for magnificent ships that sailed across stormy oceans. "Oh, how glorious to cross the blue seas!" yearned the fir tree.

When winter approached, young fir trees were cut down and carried away in carts. "Where are they going?" asked the fir tree.

"We know! We know!" chirped the sparrows through the windowpanes. "We have seen them in the grand houses of the city! They stand in the center of warm parlors, adorned with hundreds of glowing tapers, gilded apples, gingerbread, and thousands of toys!"

"Ah!" cried the fir tree, trembling with desire. "That is my destiny! That is the summit of glory!"

At Christmas, the woodman's axe bit deep into the fir tree's root. It fell with a heavy groan, feeling sharp pain as it was dragged away. In the city mansion, servants placed the tree in a wooden tub filled with sand. Golden nuts, silk ribbons, gingerbread figures, and a glittering gold star upon its highest branch completed its adornment.

When the candles were lit, the room blazed like fairy land! The children rushed into the room, danced around the tree in ecstasy, stripped it of its sweetmeats, and cheered as the old grandfather told the story of Klumpey-Dumpey. The fir tree stood in pride: "Tomorrow I shall be dressed in glory once more!"

The next morning, the footmen carried the fir tree not to the parlor, but up the dark stairs into the dusty garret, shoving it into a gloomy corner. The tree stood in darkness for months, forgotten.

The little mice visited, squeaking: "Tell us a story, old fir tree!" The tree told them of the forest sunshine, the fresh morning dew, and the glorious Christmas Eve. As he spoke, he realized for the first time how sweet and precious those forest days had been.

In spring, the servants dragged the dried, yellowed fir tree into the courtyard. The sun shone warm, the swallows sang, and children played upon the lawn. "Now life begins anew!" thought the tree, stretching its branches. But its boughs were brown and withered. A servant seized an axe, chopped the fir tree into pieces, and fed them into the brewing copper stove.

As the wood cracked in the flames, each pop sounded like a quiet sigh: "It is past! It is past! If only I had rejoiced while I had the time! Rejoice in your youth, rejoice in your fresh life while it is yours!" And the last spark flickered out into gray ashes.
moral: Live joyfully in the present moment; longing for future glory or mourning the past blinds us to life's present blessings.
